questiontext.text:
Goal

A haulage yard uses engines supplied by another company and cannot change the supplier's Engine type. Build a truck that uses the engine's existing behaviour and adds its own load.

Read
  • Struct types. Find the paragraph that defines EmbeddedField after the grammar box. What can you write as an embedded field? What name does that field receive?
  • Struct types, the example that follows that paragraph. Compare the first four declarations with the next two. Which form creates an Engine field?
  • Struct types, the two bullets on promoted methods. Which methods does S gain from an embedded T? Which more methods does *S gain?
Coming from Java

The reflex is class Truck extends Engine. When Go refuses that, the next reflex is a named field engine Engine and t.engine.Start() at every call site. Go has a third form, and the linked paragraph names the field for you.

class Truck extends Engine {
    int load;
}
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • If the truck literal in the first test fails to compile, reread which name an embedded field gets, because you do not choose that name.
  • If t.Start() fails to compile, compare the field you wrote with the four embedded fields in the spec's example struct.

testcode.text: var t Truck t.Load = 4 fmt.Println(t.Power, t.Load) fmt.Println(describe(t))
t := Truck{Engine: Engine{Power: 300}, Load: 12} t.Power = 450 fmt.Println(t.Engine.Power) fmt.Println(t.Engine.Start()) fmt.Printf("%+v\n", t)
t := Truck{Engine: Engine{Power: 250}, Load: 7} var s interface{ Start() string } = t fmt.Println(s.Start()) var sp interface{ Start() string } = &t fmt.Println(sp.Start(), describe(t))

expected.text: 250 hp running 250 hp running 250 hp, 7 t

name.text: WAT 19.2: The Override That Never Fires!

questiontext.text:
Goal

A station announcement has a fixed format with a greeting at the start. The morning announcer's script is locked. Give the night shift the same format with an evening greeting.

Read
  • Selectors. Find the paragraph beginning "A selector f may denote". What is the depth of f? What depth has a method on the outer type? What depth has a method on an embedded field?
  • Selectors, the first of the numbered rules. If both the outer and embedded types declare f, which method does x.f select?
  • Selectors, the annotated calls at the end. Which value receives M1 when p.M1() runs? Can that value access anything declared on T2?
Coming from Java

The reflex is to override Greeting on the subclass and trust the inherited Announce to dispatch back to that override. Read the linked rules to see which value the receiver inside Announce holds. Embedding leaves you restating the body, and sharing it needs the greeting passed in as a field or an interface.

class NightAnnouncer extends Announcer {
    @Override String greeting() { return "Good evening"; }
}
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • If Announce still opens with Good morning, the annotated p.M1() line shows which value the receiver holds.
  • Work out the depth of Greeting and of Announce in NightAnnouncer, then reread the first rule using those depths.

testcode.text: var a Announcer fmt.Println(a.Announce("The 9:15 to Wellington is delayed"))

expected.text: Good morning. The 9:15 to Wellington is delayed

testcode.text: var n NightAnnouncer fmt.Println(n.Announce("Last train departs")) fmt.Println(n.Announcer.Announce("Last train departs"))

expected.text: Good evening. Last train departs Good morning. Last train departs

testcode.text: n := NightAnnouncer{} fmt.Println(n.Announce("The morning papers have arrived")) fmt.Println(n.Announcer.Greeting(), n.Greeting()) fmt.Println(n.Station(), n.Announcer.Station())

expected.text: Good evening. The morning papers have arrived Good morning Good evening Wellington Central Wellington Central

questiontext.text:
Goal

A dispatch ledger arrives as one block of text. The counting house needs to read it one line at a time and report the exact number of bytes read. Write a reader that counts the bytes, then wrap bufio around it.

Read
  • bufio.NewReader. Read the signature and documentation sentence. Which type does NewReader accept? What does it return? What must your constructor provide?
  • io.Reader. Read the Read contract. Which two values does Read return? Which method must your type have before NewReader accepts it?
  • bufio.Reader.ReadString. Read the complete entry. If input ends without a newline, what value accompanies the error? What does the err != nil sentence promise about the delimiter?
Coming from Java

The decorator reflex is a subclass of FilterReader that overrides read. The loop reflex is the one below, calling readLine until it returns null. Go's ReadString has a different contract, so read its entry before you copy that loop.

BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(reader);
String line;
while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) {
    lines.add(line);
}
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • If the last line vanishes or the count comes up short, reread the ReadString sentence that begins "If ReadString encounters an error".
  • If the count is 0 after a read, check Read against the pointer-or-value receiver rule from topic 12.

testcode.text:
ls, n, err := lines("alpha
beta
") fmt.Printf("%q %d %v
", ls, n, err == nil)
ls, n, err := lines("") fmt.Printf("%q %d %v\n", ls, n, err == nil)
ls, n, err := lines("alpha\nbeta") fmt.Printf("%q %d %v\n", ls, n, err == nil)

c := NewCountingReader(ledger("kūmara")) buf := make([]byte, 4) n, err := c.Read(buf) fmt.Println(n, err == nil, c.Count()) n, err = c.Read(buf) fmt.Println(n, err == nil, c.Count()) n, err = c.Read(buf) fmt.Println(n, err == nil, c.Count()) ls, total, err := lines("kūmara

kai") fmt.Printf("%q %d %v
", ls, total, err == nil)
